titel: The euro crisis and negative interest rates
kurz: How a banking crisis became a sovereign debt crisis, what Draghi's pledge in July 2012 achieved and how eight years of negative interest rates affected German savings.

bloecke.md: In October 2009, the new Greek government revised the budget deficit for the current year from 3.7% to 12.7% of economic output. The debt ratio had risen from 104.6% to 128.5% between 2007 and 2009. Within months, the statistical correction turned into the question of whether the single currency would survive. A state with its own central bank can erode the value of its debts through inflation or devalue its currency. A member of a monetary union cannot do this. It is left with three options: cutting spending, accepting help or stopping payments. During the euro crisis, the choice between these options was fought over for six years.

bloecke.titel: Nine events of the euro crisis
bloecke.unter: Almost three years passed between the first revised deficit figure and the first effective pledge. That is how long it took for policymakers to treat the survival of the currency as a problem in its own right.

ereignisse.text: Greece revises its deficit from 3.7% to 12.7% of GDP.
Greece receives €110 billion. In November, Ireland follows with around €85 billion.
Portugal receives around €78 billion. In November, yields on ten-year Italian government bonds are above 7%, and the government resigns.
In March, private creditors waive 53.5% of the nominal value. The loss in present value is around 75%.
26 July, London. Draghi declares that the ECB will do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. The OMT programme follows in September.
For the first time, bank creditors and deposits above €100,000 are drawn on to restructure the banks.
In June, the ECB cuts the deposit facility rate to -0.10%. This marks the start of eight years of negative interest rates.
From June, the banks in Greece are closed. In the referendum on 5 July, 61.3% vote No, yet a third programme is agreed.
In August, the last programme for Greece expires. Of the €86 billion committed, €61.9 billion was paid out.

bloecke.md:
## From bank debt to government debt

The euro crisis was the continuation of the 2008 financial crisis. When governments supported their banks, the banks' losses passed into public budgets. The debt ratio of today's 27 EU member states jumped from 65.1% of GDP (2008) to 75.7% (2009). This was most evident in Ireland. The Irish state guaranteed the liabilities of its banks in 2008, and the deficit reached over 30% of economic output in 2010. Around two thirds of this was due to the bank rescue; without these costs, the deficit was around 11%.

The starting positions differed. Greece had spent too much, Ireland and Spain had a property bubble, and Italy had high legacy debt with hardly any growth. The further course was similar in all cases. As soon as investors on the bond market doubt a state's ability to pay, its interest rates rise. The higher interest rates worsen its financial position further, so that the doubt confirms itself.

bloecke.titel: The loop between banks and the state
bloecke.unter: Each arrow stands for a relationship that is plausible on its own. Together they form a feedback loop that does not stabilise without outside intervention.

knoten.notiz: they mainly hold domestic government bonds

bloecke.md:
## Rescue funds and the Troika

Article 125 TFEU (Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) prohibits the Union or a member state from being liable for the liabilities of another member state. The crisis countries nevertheless received help, through structures set up alongside the Treaty. First there were bilateral loans, then the EFSF as a temporary special purpose vehicle and, from 2012, the ESM with its own capital. Formally, these were loans subject to conditions and therefore not an assumption of debts. Legally, this difference was decisive; economically, it was small.

Compliance with the conditions was monitored by the Troika of the European Commission, the ECB and the International Monetary Fund. This body had no democratic legitimacy of its own, but in practice it had a say in pensions, tax rates and privatisations. Greece's real economic output shrank by around 26% between 2008 and 2013, and unemployment reached around 26% in 2014. It is disputed whether the conditions were too harsh or merely put together wrongly. What is undisputed is that the adjustment took longer and cost more than any draft programme had assumed.

- Ireland received around €85 billion in November 2010 because the state had taken on the costs of a banking crisis. At the end of 2013, the country returned to the capital market.
- Portugal received around €78 billion in May 2011 because of weak growth and lost competitiveness. The programme ended in 2014.
- In 2012, Spain did not receive a full programme, only a credit line for its regional savings banks. Up to €100 billion was committed, of which around 40 billion was drawn.
- In Cyprus in 2013, bank creditors and deposits above the statutory protection of €100,000 were drawn on for the first time. In Germany, this limit applies per customer and institution under Section 8 EinSiG (Deposit Guarantee Act).

## The Greek debt haircut

In March 2012 came the debt haircut that had been publicly ruled out for two years. Private creditors waived 53.5% of the nominal value of their Greek bonds. Because the new securities had longer maturities and lower interest rates, the loss measured by present value was around 75%. Those affected included banks, insurers and Greek pension funds, as well as German private investors who had bought the bonds because of the high coupons.

An investor holds Greek government bonds with a nominal value of €50,000. The investor bought them in 2010 at 70% of face value and paid €35,000 for them.

- After the exchange in March 2012, the investor owns new securities with a nominal value of €23,250 (53.5% waived).
- Measured by the present value of the old claim, around a quarter remains.
- For tax purposes, the exchange counts as a disposal under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 7 EStG (Income Tax Act). The loss goes into the general loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf) under Section 20(6) EStG. It can be offset against interest, dividends and also gains from share sales. Only losses from share sales are restricted (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG).
- The former cap on losses from bad debts and derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) in Section 20(6) EStG was abolished by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz).

The tax saving from loss offsetting makes up for a quarter of the loss at best.

Government bonds are usually low-risk, but not risk-free. Anyone who buys bonds of a state in a monetary union is lending money to a borrower without its own printing press. If fiscal consolidation cannot be pushed through politically, debt restructuring is the most likely way out.

## Draghi's pledge and the OMT programme

On 26 July 2012, ECB President Mario Draghi spoke at an investor conference in London.

bloecke.text: the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro
bloecke.quelle: Mario Draghi, Global Investment Conference, London, 26 July 2012 (ECB speech text)

bloecke.md:
In September 2012, the accompanying programme followed: Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT). It provided for unlimited purchases of short-dated government bonds, but only for countries under an ESM programme with conditions. It was never used. It worked simply because it had been announced. Investors betting against Italian or Spanish bonds now had a central bank with an unlimited balance sheet against them. Risk premiums fell without the ECB spending a single euro.

Legally, the programme remained controversial. In 2014, the Federal Constitutional Court (BVerfG) referred the question to the European Court of Justice (ECJ) for the first time in its history. The ECJ declared OMT permissible in 2015, and the Federal Constitutional Court followed in 2016, subject to conditions. Where monetary policy ends and the monetary financing of governments prohibited by Article 123 TFEU begins has never been conclusively settled.

## The negative interest rate period

After that, the crisis continued in a different form. After 2013, inflation in the euro area fell towards zero, banks in the crisis countries were hardly lending any more, and the key interest rate was already almost zero. In June 2014, the ECB cut the deposit facility rate below zero for the first time, to -0.10%. From September 2019, it stood at -0.50%. This phase only ended in July 2022. For eight years, banks therefore had to pay for holding money at the central bank.

The ECB wanted to make holding liquidity more expensive so that money would flow into loans. As a side effect, the negative rate affected all short-term interest rates in the euro area, because the deposit facility rate is their reference point. Banks offering instant-access savings accounts also base their calculations on it.

bloecke.titel: ECB deposit facility rate and yield on ten-year Bunds, 2007 to 2026
bloecke.unter: The deposit facility rate is the rate in force at the end of each year (for 2026, as of 16 September), and the Bund yield is the annual average. The annual figure for 2026 is not yet available; in August 2026, the yield was 3.18%.

bloecke.md:
## Consequences for savers

Most German retail customers never paid negative interest on their accounts. Their nominal interest rate was zero; what turned negative was the real interest rate, that is, the interest rate after deducting inflation. Between 2014 and 2022, consumer prices rose by just over 18%. Until 2020 the increase was small, and in the following two years it was 3.1% and 6.9%. A balance earning no interest lost around a sixth of its purchasing power over these nine years, even though the account statement never showed a minus.

bloecke.titel: Real return on a balance earning no interest, 2014 to 2022
bloecke.unter: At a nominal interest rate of 0%, the real return is -π/(1+π), where π is annual German inflation. In absolute terms, it is slightly below the inflation rate: in 2022, -6.5% compared with 6.9% inflation.

bloecke.titel: €10,000 without interest during the negative rate period

bloecke.md:
## Consequences for the banks

A bank earns mainly from the difference between the interest rates for short-term refinancing and the interest rates for long-term lending. With a deposit facility rate of -0.50% and a yield on ten-year German federal bonds of -0.51% as the 2020 annual average, this difference had mathematically disappeared. The institutions hit hardest were those with lots of deposits and little lending business, in Germany above all Sparkassen (savings banks) and cooperative banks. They paid the negative rate on their excess liquidity but could hardly pass it on to retail customers. The institutions responded with account fees, custody charges (Verwahrentgelte) on larger balances and mergers. From October 2019, the ECB exempted part of the reserves from the negative rate.

From 2022, the sign reversed. The same excess liquidity that had cost money for eight years earned 4.00% from September 2023. Banks' net interest income jumped, while interest rates on savings followed with a delay and not in full. This asymmetry repeats itself in every interest rate cycle.

bloecke.titel: Negative interest in the German Civil Code
bloecke.md: The basic rate of interest (Basiszinssatz) under Section 247 BGB (Civil Code) follows the ECB's main refinancing rate and only changes on 1 January and 1 July. From July 2016 to December 2022, it stood at -0.88%. Under Section 288 BGB, default interest owed by consumers is the basic rate of interest plus 5 percentage points, and in business transactions plus 9 percentage points. A consumer in payment default therefore owed 4.12% at that time. Since 1 July 2026, the basic rate of interest has been 1.52%, so default interest for consumers is 6.52%. In this way, changes in monetary policy reach civil law with a delay of up to six months, without any vote being taken on them.

T2 (TARGET2 until 2023) is the Eurosystem's real-time payment system. If a customer in Spain transfers money to a German bank, this creates a liability of the Spanish central bank towards the ECB and a claim of the same size for the Bundesbank. These positions record cross-border payments in central bank money in the accounts. They are not a specially granted loan.

The balances grew strongly in the crisis years because capital flowed from the periphery to Germany and banks no longer funded each other. In this respect, they indicate how much confidence there is in the banking system. The reading that Germany secretly granted loans that could be called in is wrong. Such positions arise in every national payment system, but are not reported by region there. They would only turn into a real loss if the monetary union broke apart.

## The situation in 2026

The ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026, after the central bank raised it in June and September 2026. The German inflation rate was 2.9% in August 2026. The Eurosystem's balance sheet has shrunk from its peak of €8,836 billion (June 2022) to €5,911 billion (11 September 2026). That is still around five times the level at the start of 2007. The government debt ratio of the euro area, with its 21 members, is 88.9% of GDP (first quarter of 2026), and Germany's is 64.4%. Most members have been above the Maastricht reference value of 60% for a long time.

Assume €20,000 at 2.50% interest, without church tax. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG) has already been used up by other income.

- The interest income is €500.00.
- The flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer, 25%, Section 32d(1) EStG) and the solidarity surcharge together amount to 26.375%, that is, €131.88.
- €368.12 remains net, which is 1.84%.
- With 2.9% inflation, the balance loses €580 in purchasing power.

Overall, this results in a real loss of around €212, just over 1% of the balance. The gap to the negative interest rate period is considerably smaller than the headline “interest is back at last” suggests.

Under the nominal value principle (Nominalwertprinzip), the flat-rate withholding tax is levied on nominal interest rather than on the real return. If inflation is as high as the interest rate, you pay tax on a gain that does not exist in real terms. An account without price fluctuations is therefore not risk-free. Its risk just does not show up in the account statement.

1. For balances, calculate with the real interest rate after tax rather than with the advertised nominal rate.
2. Statutory deposit protection of €100,000 per customer and institution (Section 8 EinSiG) is an upper limit rather than a target. Cyprus in 2013 showed what can happen above it.
3. A conspicuously high coupon on a government bond reflects the probability of default estimated by the market and is no extra return. Greek bonds yielded double digits before the debt haircut, and the default happened.

mitnehmen: As soon as the state is liable for its banks, a banking crisis becomes a sovereign debt crisis, as the rise in the EU debt ratio in 2008/09 from 65.1% to 75.7% of GDP shows.
A state in a monetary union lacks its own printing press, and in the Greek debt haircut of 2012, private creditors lost 53.5% of the nominal value and around 75% of the present value.
Draghi's pledge of July 2012 worked through its credibility alone, because the associated OMT programme was never used.

During the eight years of negative interest rates, most German savers paid no negative interest on their accounts, but between 2014 and 2022, balances earning no interest lost around a sixth of their purchasing power.
Even in 2026, 2.50% interest after flat-rate withholding tax and with 2.9% inflation results in a real loss of around 1%.

begriffe.text: Body made up of the European Commission, the ECB and the IMF that negotiated the conditions of the aid programmes during the euro crisis and monitored compliance with them.
Partial waiver of claims by a state's creditors. In Greece in 2012, private creditors waived 53.5% of the nominal value, and the loss in present value was around 75%.
Programme announced by the ECB in 2012 for the unlimited purchase of short-dated government bonds, tied to reform conditions. It was never used and worked through the announcement alone.

Interest rate that banks receive or pay on overnight deposits with the central bank, in effect the key interest rate of the Eurosystem. It was negative from June 2014 to July 2022 and has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026.
Claim or liability of a national central bank in the Eurosystem's payment system. The balance arises automatically as the counter-entry to cross-border payments and is not a specially granted loan.
Interest rate under Section 247 BGB, adjusted every six months to the ECB's main refinancing rate. It is the basis for default interest under Section 288 BGB.
